(1) Decide what plants you want to grow.

(2) Figure out roughly the size of plot you'll need to grow those plants, or alternatively, if your plot size is limited and you already know it, use that to determine what you can grow.

(3) Roughly mark out your plot and till the earth up; if you have thick sod to remove, you're going to have a big job. The best thing you can do if you want to be a hobby gardener is get a decent little rototiller. It will save you so much work.

(4) As far as when to plant, a rough guideline is to wait until after the last frost; in Texas that is going to be probably mid-March; in Michigan, I plant in May. A killing frost can ruin your garden, so the best bet is to play it safe and wait until you can reasonably expect nighttime lows to not dip below freezing. If you do get your plants in the ground and the weather is issuing a frost advisory, whether early season or late season, cover your plants. They make frost covers that you can buy or you can make them with your own material.

Many people will get their seedlings started indoors using growing lights, and that gives them a head start, after which you can then transfer them outdoors after the threat of frost is gone. This also has the advantage of letting you carefully control the growing conditions and soil nutrients. But it isn't necessary if you are a first-timer. If you aren't starting your plants indoors, chances are good you'll be planting from seed, or buying young plants from your local greenhouse.

(5) Put the plants in the ground; if you did not start your plants indoors yourself, and you are buying plants from a greenhouse, for example, all you have to do is remove the plants from their trays, use your fingers to break up the root matrix a little bit, and then put them in the ground about as deep as the root system. If you are planting seed, like cucumbers for instance, use a hoe and make yourself a little "trough" in the dirt the full length of your row, abut 3/4 inches deep. You can actually use your hand for this. Seeds don't need to go deep; too deep and you won't germinate. Sprinkle the seeds in your shallow little row-trough, and push the dirt over them.

(6) Do not crowd the garden. You can find online some general guidelines for any type of plant that tell you how much area they typically require to be healthy; don't crowd.

(7) If things get bone dry, i.e. the soil in your garden about an inch down (stick your thumb in) is very dry, and you notice your plants mid-summer are looking "sad", hit them with a shower from the hose and help them out. You'll develop a fast sense for a plant that looks healthy and hydrated. Some people in areas with hot, dry summers will by sprinkler hoses and run these through the garden. That way, if you have a dry run of weather, you can just turn the faucet on at the house and let the sprinkler hoses do the work for a couple hours. It all depends on how dry it is. Some plants do better being "tested" or "stressed" a little.

(8) As far as soil amendments, I wouldn't worry about this until you get a season of planting under your belt. If you want to initially see what your soil quality is, most localities have some kind of soil testing service available. For example, my town's local elevator will send your dirt samples to university to be lab tested and they'll generate a report about your soil. You can go buy the kit at the elevator and take it home to collect your sample. You may, or may not, want to do this your first year. I probably wouldn't. As a roughshod rule, the blacker your dirt, the healthier the soil. Try not to plant in something that is really sandy, or mostly clay.

(9) As far as fertilizing, a lot of this will depend upon the soil (as mentioned above) and what your soil is missing. Certain plants also like certain nutrients more than others (you can find tips on plant-specific fertilization techniques online all over the place). One simple and basic type of fertilization that helps build your soil is to compost your yard refuse (leaves) and then till this compost into the top soil of your garden prior to planting. Additionally, you could also use leaves or straw or wood chips as a mulch once your plants start to come up, just around the base of the plants.

In general, plants prefer more nitrogen during the "vegetative" part of the season, when they are not flowering yet, but are starting to sprawl out. Later they prefer more phosphorus and potassium when they start to flower. Personally, I wouldn't get too into the minutiae and hair-splitting my first time. If it were me, I'd get a pack of Miracle Grow and water your plants with a little of this once weekly or bi-weekly, especially during the vegetative, pre-bloom phase. You can start to learn about fertilization as you go, and improve.

(10) Weed your garden at least weekly.

(11) Lastly, once your plants begin to produce, keep them picked. As long as you are taking the fruit off the plants, they'll keep producing. But when you leave them on the vine to get really large, your plants will slow down on production very quickly. You'll be amazed at how productive the plants can be. You'll want to check them around every other day and get the veg that is appropriately sized off of the vine. That will keep them cooking for most of the harvest season, until a frost comes and kills them.

I would recommend Hugelkultur. First off, above ground gardens are just easier to take care of. Plants only need about a foot of soil so there is no good reason to spend a lot of money filling in the bottom 2/3 of a 3 ft raised bed. With Hugelkultur you fill the bottom of the beds in with logs, sticks, leaves and other garden debris, it breaks down over time releasing nutrients and saved tons of money on soil.

Hugelkultur means hill culture or hill mound. In short, this is a type of gardening where you create the base with large logs. You pile other compostable materials on top of the logs into a hill or mound. From there, you cover them with soil and plant your vegetables in this type of bed.

I also wouldn't waste money on building raised beds from lumber, it's expensive and breaks down after a few years.
